r: Introduction to Environmental Engineering covers materials balances, pollution overview, water/wastewater treatment basics, sustainability, and life-cycle assessment as a gateway conceptual course. Current tools can already draft LCA summaries or explain a treatment train at a survey level, but the course's actual work task is building the mass-balance reasoning and pollutant-classification judgment students carry into later design work, not producing polished text. Task-exposure research finds science and critical-thinking skills negatively associated with exposure, which fits this course's emphasis on conceptual framing over rote output. Verification burden is high: misjudging pollutant fate or treatment adequacy has real health and regulatory consequences, so a human instructor must still validate reasoning. Realized automatable displacement of the course's instrumental function is low today; adoption of AI tools for this kind of foundational conceptual instruction remains limited and unevenly diffused across programs.

Within five years, capability trend data (METR/Epoch task-horizon doubling roughly every 4-7 months) suggests AI systems will handle mass-balance calculations, pollutant-fate estimates, and sustainability/LCA drafting with much greater fluency, pushing raw task automatability toward the higher end of the scale. But two dampeners hold instrumental need higher than capability alone implies: environmental and public-health judgments carry high error costs requiring an expert who actually understands the material to check outputs, and this course sits inside ABET's engineering-topic and math/science credit-hour floor, which mandates the subject sequence even though it does not name this specific course. EVE 1040 is also the direct prerequisite for EVE 2000 and EVE 3000, making it foundational scaffolding for the rest of the environmental engineering curriculum. These constraints cap the rating at Medium rather than allowing it to track capability upward unchecked.

At a ten-year horizon, further capability gains are plausible but genuinely uncertain, and diffusion research (Census BTOS) shows adoption consistently lags raw capability even in commercial settings, let alone accredited curricula with structural inertia. The binding constraints identified at five years persist: ABET's engineering-topic and math/science hour floor still requires this course sequence, and EVE 1040 remains the entry point that EVE 2000's lab work and EVE 3000's concepts course build on, so removing it would require restructuring the accredited degree plan itself, not just substituting a tool. Verification burden for environmental and public-health judgments is unlikely to fully disappear even as tools improve, since error costs remain asymmetric. A confident point prediction is not warranted, but nothing in the visible institutional or pedagogical structure suggests the instrumental need collapses to Low by 2036; Medium remains the defensible ceiling.
EVE 1040.d: Students in this course are introduced to environmental engineering. They learn about the fundamentals of environmental engineering. An introduction to materials balances, environmental pollution, and water/wastewater treatment will be presented in this course. An overview of environmental impacts, sustainability, and life cycle assessment will be also discussed in this course. Students will be familiar with emerging trends in environmental engineering.

EVE 1215.d: In this course students study solid modeling fundamentals, geometric constructions, multi-view projections, section views, and dimensioning using adequate CAD software.

EVE 2000.d: Students learn the standard laboratory analysis of water and wastewater samples for the measurements of inorganic and organic contaminants. Students are prepared to analyze and monitor samples utilizing laboratory equipment. EVE 2150.d: In this course, students study the principles of mechanics of static systems in two- and three-dimensions: static equilibrium of particles and rigid bodies; section properties; internal forces in statically determinate trusses and beams; friction; and virtual work.

EVE 2250.d: This course will engage students with global engineering challenges and build awareness of engineering practices abroad through participation in an international engineering project.

EVE 3500.d: Students apply the critical processes controlling contaminants and their movement in the environmental media. EVE 4160.d: Students in this course are introduced to the basic principles of soil behavior and their use in geotechnical and geoenvironmental engineering. This course covers soil formation, soil characterization and classification, engineering properties of soil, compaction, fluid flow in soil, stresses in soil, consolidation and settlement, shear strength, and lateral earth pressures. Students are introduced to soil improvement and remediation strategies and the design of earth retaining structures. This course contains a laboratory that covers common geotechnical tests such as sieve analysis, Atterberg limits, hydraulic conductivity, and soil shear strength.

r: This course teaches design of water distribution systems, drainage channels, hydraulic structures, stormwater collection, and pipeline networks, plus rainfall-runoff analysis and evapotranspiration estimation. EVE 4400.d: Students in this course are introduced to water resources engineering. They learn about the fundamentals of water resources engineering. EVE 4420.d: This course offers a broad overview of wetland landscapes. Topics include: (1) Spatial distribution (local and national), (2) variations in wetlands topology (salt-water versus fresh- water and warmer versus colder climates), (3) relationships between wetlands (migratory flight paths), (4) wetlands ecosystems (5) human impacts on wetlands, (6) federal, state, and local wetlands regulations, and (7) international wetlands problems. EVE 4450.d: In this course students are introduced to applications of wood design in engineering. Analysis and design of wood structures is presented.

EVE 4500.d: The course (EVE 4500) aims to cover solid-waste characteristics, recycling, landfilling, incineration, hazardous waste characteristics, prevention, and physical and chemical treatment.
